stories.title: The Middle East conflict spreads to Yemen and Gulf shipping
body: A Saudi-led coalition launched major strikes across Houthi-held areas of Yemen, saying it targeted military facilities. Houthi authorities reported at least 17 deaths, including people killed at a factory in Hodeida. In parallel, Iran claimed to have struck a US base in the Gulf, while Bahrain and Kuwait reported aerial threats. These are reports from participants in an active conflict, and not every operational or casualty claim has been independently confirmed.

The wider significance is that the violence is no longer confined to a single front. The Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb are vital to energy supply and commercial shipping; attacks, even without a formal blockade, can increase shipping risk, insurance costs and the price of imported goods. India has particular exposure through energy imports and maritime employment. The story to watch is whether commercial passage becomes more disrupted and whether regional governments can contain further escalation.

stories.title: Xi and Putin gather in Shenzhen ahead of talks with Trump
body: Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen ahead of an expected trilateral meeting with US President Donald Trump. Xi criticised trade protectionism and Putin attacked Western sanctions. The proposed talks are expected to cover a range of contentious issues, including Ukraine, the conflict involving Iran, trade and arms control; their outcomes were not yet known at the edition cutoff.

The significance is not merely diplomatic theatre. These powers can influence security, trade and technology rules that affect countries outside the room. India is one such country, with relationships spanning the Quad, Russia and China. A leaders’ meeting should not be treated as a breakthrough by itself: an agreed policy, a practical concession, or a verifiable change in behaviour would be the consequential result.

stories.title: Denial of aid to children in conflicts is sharply higher in UN records
body: A Save the Children analysis of UN-verified incidents found 8,322 cases of denial of humanitarian assistance to children in 2025, compared with 509 in 2015. The occupied Palestinian territories accounted for the largest number in 2025, followed by other conflict zones. These are verified recorded incidents, not a full count of every instance of aid obstruction around the world.

The figures illustrate how civilians can be harmed not only by attacks but also by the loss of food, medicine and essential services. Even where humanitarian law is clear, access on the ground depends on belligerents, border controls, security and the capacity of relief groups. Changes in reporting and verification capacity complicate decade-long comparisons, but the scale of the documented increase is significant.

sources.label: Save the Children report via coverage

stories.title: Nvidia suspends shipments of some US-approved AI chips to China
body: Nvidia says it is no longer shipping certain licensed Hopper-generation data-centre processors to China. Interim CEO Colette Kress disclosed about $2.4 billion in sales of the relevant licensed products in the quarter ended 25 October. The firm has not fully specified how long the shipment interruption will last or how much is attributable to government rules versus commercial demand.

The bigger story is the growing entanglement of AI infrastructure and national industrial policy. Washington is tightening controls on advanced computing, while Beijing wants to build competing domestic chip capabilities. For suppliers and data-centre operators, even a product cleared for sale can remain exposed to shifting policy and strategic competition. Lost shipments are not the same as an end to China’s access to computing, nor proof that controls are achieving all their objectives.

stories.title: A Deutsche Bank document leak puts high-risk client controls under scrutiny
body: An investigative collaboration, including Newslaundry, examined more than 15 million leaked Deutsche Bank records. One report identifies about $582 million in suspicious payments associated with Jeffrey Epstein. The archive also contains internal risk assessments and correspondence about other wealthy and politically connected clients. Reuters said it could not immediately independently verify the full leaked archive; Deutsche Bank has pointed to improvements in controls and said much of the conduct described is historical.

The important question is whether banks can apply anti-financial-crime safeguards consistently when dealing with powerful or profitable customers. A flagged transaction is not proof of a crime, but ignored alerts or inadequate escalation can expose weaknesses in supervision. This is a long-form investigation worth reading directly, rather than reducing it to a definitive verdict on every person mentioned.

stories.title: Russian strikes leave Kyiv struggling with power outages as winter approaches
body: Repeated Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have left Kyiv enduring severe power interruptions as colder weather approaches. A Guardian report describes residents managing disrupted electricity and heat alongside growing criticism of Mayor Vitali Klitschko over the city’s preparations. Those criticisms concern preparedness and responsibility; they should not obscure that attacks on infrastructure are the immediate cause of much of the damage.

The larger issue is how energy systems become a front in a prolonged war. Electricity outages affect water pumping, hospitals, lifts, public transport and livelihoods, with the greatest burden often falling on people who cannot arrange private backup power. Repairs can restore service but repeated attacks can undo progress. The distinction worth watching is between damage caused by new strikes and preventable weaknesses in local preparedness—both require evidence, and assigning responsibility remains politically contested.

stories.title: Russian strategic bombers fly across East Asia and land in Vietnam
body: Two Russian Tu-95 strategic bombers made an unusual long-range deployment to Da Nang, Vietnam, after a flight that prompted air-defence responses and concern in Japan and Taiwan. Reuters reported that Japan protested suspected Russian aircraft entering its territorial airspace in a related incident, while aircraft movements also drew scrutiny around Taiwan and South Korea. Reports of an aircraft entering an air-defence identification zone should not automatically be described as a violation of sovereign airspace: they are legally different.

The broader significance is strategic signalling ahead of meetings involving the Russian, Chinese and American leaders. Deploying long-range aircraft tests logistics, demonstrates reach and draws regional military attention without necessarily signalling an imminent attack. Analysts differ on how closely the route was coordinated politically and what Moscow intended to convey. The practical consequences depend on whether the deployment remains a one-off demonstration or becomes part of a sustained pattern of regional military operations.

stories.title: UK inflation rises to 3.6%, driven in part by fuel prices
body: Britain’s Consumer Prices Index rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September, according to the Office for National Statistics. Petrol and diesel prices made an important contribution. The higher headline figure does not imply that all goods and services are becoming more expensive at the same rate.

For households, fuel and energy costs transmit into transport, heating and eventually business prices. For the Bank of England, a renewed inflation rise complicates decisions on interest rates at a time when some consumers and borrowers are already under pressure. The distinction between volatile energy inflation and more persistent underlying pressures will matter for future policy.

sources.label: Office for National Statistics · October CPI

stories.title: The NHS plans to leave Palantir’s data platform—but not until 2029
body: The UK government says Palantir’s role supplying the NHS Federated Data Platform will end in March 2029, rather than exercising a break option that might have brought the contract to an end earlier. Ministers argue a transition and new procurement need time; critics question why the supplier should remain so embedded for longer. Novara Media has reported on resistance among NHS staff and on whether hospitals cited as success stories are actually using the platform extensively.

This is a case study in the difficulty of changing technology suppliers in public services. Procurement, dependence on proprietary systems, claims of operational benefits and trust in health-data governance all have to be assessed separately. An announced end date is not evidence that a replacement is ready, and criticism of the vendor does not on its own establish what the existing platform has or has not achieved.

stories.title: Researchers will evaluate the UK social-media restrictions affecting under-16s
body: Wellcome is funding ten research teams with £9.3 million to study the effects of forthcoming social-media restrictions on more than 300,000 young people. The projects will examine mental health, sleep, relationships and other outcomes, with some studies comparing behaviour before and after the changes.

The policy debate has often moved faster than the evidence. Researchers need to understand benefits, unintended effects, differences between groups and whether restrictions displace use into less visible spaces. This announcement is a study launch, not evidence that the ban works or fails; its value will lie in the quality of the resulting comparisons.

stories.title: NHS patient-record snooping incidents expose a distinct privacy problem
body: Freedom-of-information responses documented more than 3,000 confirmed occasions of NHS staff improperly accessing patient records across several years. Not every trust supplied complete comparable figures, so the count is not a national total of all misconduct. Some cases involve staff accessing records without a legitimate medical reason.

Healthcare data security is about internal access governance as much as external hackers or technology suppliers. Systems need effective audit trails, detection, sanctions and clear patient remedies. This is related to wider public trust in digitised health services, but is not proof of wrongdoing by any particular outside software vendor.

stories.title: Labour faces renewed pressure to define Britain’s long-term relationship with the EU
body: Former foreign secretary David Lammy has called on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to campaign at the next election on a commitment to rejoin the European Union. The intervention follows Burnham’s criticism of Brexit’s economic and diplomatic consequences, but his government has delayed setting out specific long-term options while preparing for a major UK–EU summit. Lammy’s position is a political proposal, not an adopted government policy.

The bigger question is whether Britain can deepen economic integration with the EU without reopening the political disputes that shaped the original Brexit negotiations. Trade barriers, standards, migration rules and access to European programmes affect businesses and households, but full membership would involve broader obligations and renewed democratic debate. Divisions within Labour, competing priorities in Brussels and concerns among Leave-supporting constituencies make any shift far from automatic.

stories.title: Reform’s promised local-government efficiency drive has yielded limited savings
body: A Guardian examination of English councils led by Reform UK reports that the party’s promised cost-cutting drive has not, so far, produced faster or deeper savings than those achieved by comparable authorities. The party had promoted a programme modelled on Elon Musk’s US government-efficiency initiative after its local-election gains. Interviews and comparative evidence suggest a gap between the rhetoric of immediate administrative overhaul and what councils have actually delivered.

The story matters because local-government budgets are constrained by statutory obligations, service demand and existing contracts. Reducing expenditure is not simply a matter of removing jobs or announcing targets: cuts can shift costs, reduce service quality or take longer to implement than promised. A short early performance period does not establish what may happen throughout a full council term, but the available results provide a test of a specific political claim about rapid savings.

stories.title: A sweeping review of youth employment proposes deep changes to welfare and training
body: A review led by Alan Milburn proposes wide-ranging measures to address the UK’s large population of young people not in education, employment or training (NEET). Recommendations include expanded apprenticeships, more specialised career support and wider changes across schools, health services and benefits. The review also contemplates substantial changes to disability-related support, prompting concern from critics about potential losses of financial security.

The larger issue is whether unemployment among young people is best addressed through skills and hiring incentives, conditional welfare reform, or stronger support for health, housing and access to work. The report recognises structural barriers such as poverty and ill health but couples new opportunities with tougher conditions. Its recommendations are not enacted policy. The government’s response—and independent assessment of potential effects on disabled and low-income young people—will matter more than the review’s scale alone.

sources.label: UK review · From a Welfare State to a Working State

stories.title: Democrats secure a 56–44 US Senate majority after Alaska result
body: Mary Peltola defeated Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in Alaska, completing the Democrats’ ninth Republican-held Senate pickup of the 2026 midterms. The incoming Senate is set to have a 56–44 Democratic majority. Democrats have also won control of the House, sharply changing the balance of power in Congress.

The result constrains President Trump’s legislative agenda and creates more opportunities for congressional oversight, but it does not transfer executive authority to Congress. Control of committees, spending measures and subpoena power will matter. The figures describe the incoming Congress, which takes office in January, not the chamber’s composition on election night.

stories.title: Congressional investigations of Trump may face constitutional barriers
body: Democrats preparing to control congressional committees have said they will pursue broad investigations of President Trump and his administration. Reuters examined how Supreme Court precedents on congressional subpoenas, presidential records and separation of powers might affect those efforts. Congress can seek documents and testimony, but legal enforcement can be slow and contested.

The key question is whether the incoming majority can exercise oversight effectively when the executive branch resists. Political control of a committee does not automatically guarantee access to every record; equally, the existence of legal limits does not negate Congress’s investigative powers. The story is about institutional checks, not a completed finding of misconduct.

stories.title: A $50bn air-traffic funding request meets resistance after mass flight disruption
body: The Trump administration is seeking roughly $50 billion for air-traffic-control reforms and airport improvements after a nationwide ground stop caused more than 18,000 flight cancellations. The request expanded from a $30 billion proposal, and some Republican senators have challenged the scale and mix of spending.

The aviation system has long-running modernisation problems, but a high-profile failure is not enough to settle which investments are most effective. Lawmakers want accountability for earlier funding and clearer priorities. The distinction between urgent safety improvements and broader airport upgrades will shape the debate over who pays and how quickly repairs can be made.

stories.title: Appeals court blocks removal of transgender service members while litigation continues
body: A divided federal appeals court blocked the US military from forcing more than two dozen transgender service members out while litigation over the Trump administration’s policy continues. The ruling follows earlier findings that the policy was unlawfully discriminatory; the administration is seeking further Supreme Court review. The order concerns the affected personnel and ongoing proceedings, not a final nationwide resolution of every challenge to military service rules.

The case tests the extent to which the executive branch can set personnel standards for the armed forces while remaining subject to constitutional protections. Supporters of the policy frame it as a question of military readiness and administrative discretion; challengers say exclusion based on gender identity is discriminatory. The court’s interim protection preserves the status of the service members involved while the merits and procedural questions continue to be contested.

stories.title: Supreme Court leaves in place a ruling against cancellation of university research grants
body: The US Supreme Court declined to hear the Trump administration’s appeal concerning the cancellation of about $59 million in grants to researchers at the University of California, Berkeley. The Ninth Circuit had found that the grant terminations were likely unlawful viewpoint discrimination because they targeted work described as supporting diversity, equity and inclusion. The research covered fields including medicine, climate policy, water management and the humanities.

The significance lies in the boundary between government power to set funding priorities and constitutional limits on penalising disfavoured viewpoints. Declining review leaves the lower-court ruling in place; it is not a fresh Supreme Court ruling deciding all disputes about DEI-related funding. Academic institutions and federal agencies will be watching how this reasoning affects other grant challenges and the conditions under which scientific work is financed.

stories.title: US officials say recent major technology outages are not known to be connected
body: A succession of disruptions affecting air travel, banking, online services and government communications has prompted public speculation about a coordinated cyberattack. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials had no evidence linking the incidents to one another or to a malicious actor. The organisations involved have attributed various failures to technical problems. Those statements reflect the available evidence, not proof that future investigations cannot uncover additional causes.

The bigger story is the fragility of highly interconnected services. A problem in one platform or update can interfere with critical activities far beyond the original system. Similar-looking failures may be unrelated, and treating coincidence as proof of sabotage can distract from engineering, maintenance and transparency. The useful follow-up is whether operators publish credible root-cause analyses and what they change to prevent repeat outages—not whether a dramatic common explanation circulates online.

stories.title: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary forces amid violence over Hasina’s planned return
body: Bangladesh deployed hundreds of paramilitary personnel on 18 November as violence intensified ahead of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s stated intention to return from exile in India in December. Reuters reported crude-bomb explosions and arson incidents across numerous districts, with people killed or injured in separate attacks. The government has declined her request for new identity and travel documents, while her banned Awami League has called for protests, including a planned nationwide shutdown.

The upheaval exposes how unsettled Bangladesh’s post-2024 political order remains. Hasina’s attempted return is an immediate trigger, but disputes about political legitimacy, prosecutions and the right to organise run deeper. Government officials blame overseas party figures for encouraging violence; these are allegations, not proof of responsibility for every incident. The next test is whether security operations can protect civilians without further narrowing political space. India also has a direct diplomatic stake because Hasina has been living there.

stories.title: Bangladesh’s garment workers press for higher wages as factories shut
body: Workers in Bangladesh’s export-oriented ready-made garment industry have continued demonstrations across Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk 30,000. The Daily Star reported clashes with police, road blockades and disruptions to factory production. One report estimated that close to 450 factories faced a production halt on 17 November; industrial police said 25 factories in the Savar–Ashulia area were not operating on 18 November. Those counts cover different locations and reporting periods, not a single national total.

The bigger picture is a dispute about how the economic returns from Bangladesh’s garment exports are shared. The sector is central to export earnings and millions of livelihoods, but manufacturers also face energy costs and pressure from overseas buyers. Parliamentarians have alleged political orchestration of the unrest, while workers and labour organisations have raised wages and working conditions. Those are distinct claims: allegations about who may be exploiting protests do not establish that workers’ wage demands are illegitimate. The test is whether credible negotiations can address pay, workplace safety and the viability of factories without suppressing lawful organising.
